draft.title: The sample proportion
card: The sample proportion is p̂ = X ÷ n, where X is the number in the sample with a feature and n is the sample size.
If we take many random samples of the same size n from a population with proportion p, the value of p̂ changes each time.
For large n, the distribution of p̂ is roughly normal, with mean p and standard deviation √(p(1 − p)/n).
Example: p = 0.4 and n = 100. The standard deviation is √(0.4 × 0.6/100) = √0.0024, which is about 0.049. So p̂ is centred on 0.4 and usually lies within about 0.1 of it.
draft.remember: p̂ varies between samples, and for large n it is roughly normal and centred on p.

a.q: Many random samples of size 100 are taken from a population where p = 0.4. Around which value are the p̂ values centred?
a.why: The distribution of p̂ is centred on the population proportion p, which is 0.4. The value 0.04 mixes up the mean with a spread-type value, and the sample size is not a proportion.
a.clue: Where does the distribution of p̂ sit compared with p?

b.q: A factory has a fault rate of p = 0.2. Random samples of 400 items are tested. What is the standard deviation of p̂?
b.why: The standard deviation is √(0.2 × 0.8/400) = √0.0004 = 0.02. The answer 0.0004 is the variance, because the square root step was skipped. The answer 0.16 is just 0.2 × 0.8.
b.clue: Use √(p(1 − p)/n) and finish with the square root.

check.summary: No problems found. The card's formulas and worked example are correct, and both questions have a single right answer (0.4 and 0.02) that matches the explanations.

final.title: The sample proportion
card: The sample proportion is \(\hat{p} = \frac{X}{n}\), where \(X\) is the number in the sample with a feature and \(n\) is the sample size.
If we take many random samples of the same size \(n\) from a population with proportion \(p\), the value of \(\hat{p}\) changes each time.
For large \(n\), the distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is roughly normal, with mean \(p\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}\).

Example: \(p = 0.4\) and \(n = 100\). The standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\frac{0.4 \times 0.6}{100}} = \sqrt{0.0024}\), which is about 0.049. So \(\hat{p}\) is centred on 0.4 and usually lies within about 0.1 of it.
final.remember: \(\hat{p}\) varies between samples, and for large \(n\) it is roughly normal and centred on \(p\).
